analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to make taxpayer-funded research papers free online within six months.
analysis.headline: The bill, offering free public access to federally funded research, was introduced by a bipartisan group of four senators but never received a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every federal agency that spends more than $100 million a year on outside research to put the resulting peer-reviewed papers online for free within six months of publication, in a permanent public repository. Today, taxpayers fund this research but often must pay journal subscription companies or per-article fees to read the results. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, patients, teachers, students, small businesses, and scientists who currently pay to read research their tax dollars already paid for; free online access removes the paywall.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and researchers seeking funded research

how_it_helps.text: Each agency with over $100 million in outside research spending must create a policy providing free online access to final peer-reviewed papers from federally funded research no later than six months after publication [S2] [S3].
Papers must be kept in a stable digital repository with long-term free public access, and agencies must publish annual reports and public lists showing which funded papers were made accessible [S3].

The bill's findings state that federal research is funded with the expectation that results will be shared to advance science and improve people's lives, and that the internet makes this possible for every scientist, physician, educator, and citizen [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Academic journal publishers, whose business of charging universities and readers for subscription access to federally funded research would lose part of its exclusive control; they could also face shorter revenue windows from a six-month embargo.

drawbacks.text: Requiring free access within six months of publication shortens the period during which journal publishers can charge for the newest papers, which publishers argue threatens the subscription revenue that funds peer review and journal editing; the six-month window is shorter than the twelve-month standard later adopted by federal agencies [S3].

The bill leaves patent and copyright law untouched and excludes patentable discoveries, books that generate royalties, and classified research, so it does not resolve broader disputes over ownership of federally funded inventions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public gain is broad and real: research already paid for with tax dollars becomes readable by the doctors, students, and businesses who use it. The cost falls on a specific industry, journal publishers, whose subscription model would lose exclusive control over publicly funded papers; a six-month embargo is aggressive but the bill preserves copyright and patent rights, so publishers keep a window of paid access.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing or vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Cornyn introduced the bill on February 9, 2012, joined by Senators Wyden and Hutchison, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S5].
The bill had three cosponsors, two Democrats and one Republican, alongside its Republican sponsor [S4].
No further action was recorded after the committee referral; the Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Journal publishers kept their paywall-based control over federally funded research, and taxpayers continued paying twice, once in taxes and again in subscription or per-article fees.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as a cosponsor.

for.name: Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.

against.name: Academic journal publishers
against.what_they_did: Opposed open-access mandates for federally funded research, funding a lobbying campaign that same Congress for legislation to block such requirements.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor from Texas recruited a Democratic cosponsor from Oregon and another Texas Republican at introduction, and the three later cosponsors split two Democrats and one Republican.

industries.note: These companies sell universities and readers subscription access to papers describing research taxpayers already funded; the bill would force free online versions within six months, cutting into their exclusive control of the newest results. Their interest ran against the public's interest in reading what it had paid for.
Institutions pay large journal subscription fees, and their researchers would gain wider readership for federally funded work under a free repository system.
